subtopic: RESIGNATION OF DONALD GORDON AS CHAIRMAN- APPOINTMENT OF K. W. TAYLOR

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RESIGNATION OF DONALD GORDON AS CHAIRMAN- APPOINTMENT OF K. W. TAYLOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief statement regarding the chairmanship of the -wartime prices and trade board which, because of its importance and interest, I have felt should be given in the first instance to parliament.
After five and a half years of service as chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, Mr. Donald Gordon has asked to be relieved of his duties in order to return on a full time basis to his position as deputy governor of the Bank of Canada. The recent appointment of Mr. Graham F. Towers as Canadian executive director of the international bank for reconstruction and development lends a certain urgency to Mr. Gordon's request.
The government, after careful consideration, has reached the conclusion that plans for the orderly decontrol of prices are sufficiently

Wartime Prices and Trade Board
advanced to make it possible to meet Mr. Gordon's wishes without the public interest being adversely affected. Mr. Gordon's resignation has accordingly been accepted to take effect on April 15. He will be succeeded as chairman of the wartime prices and trade board by the now deputy chairman, Mr. Kenneth W. Taylor. Mr. Taylor has been with the board since its establishment in 1939.
I should not like the acceptance of Mr. Donald Gordon's resignation to pass without expressing the government's deep appreciation -which I am sure will be shared by hon. members of both Houses of Parliament-of the exceptional contribution made by Mr. Gordon, as chairman of the prices board, to the effective economic mobilization of Canada's resources during the war and, since the termination of hostilities, to an orderly transition to a peacetime economy in our country.
The success of Canada's campaign against inflation during the war and in its subsequent control owes very much to the untiring devotion. integrity and courage displayed by Mr. Donald Gordon in the discharge of the arduous duties of chairman of the wartime prices and trade board. I -feel I may speak for the Canadian people as a whole when, at this moment of his retirement, I express to Mr. Gordon our thanks for the invaluable service he has rendered our country at a time of its greatest need.

subtopic: RESIGNATION OF DONALD GORDON AS CHAIRMAN- APPOINTMENT OF K. W. TAYLOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think this occasion should be allowed to pass without someone on this side of the house associating us with what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said. I feel that Mr. Donald Gordon has been subjected to a great deal of criticism and sometimes we felt that the criticism might have some basis. However I believe (he whole country has been well served by the job Mr. Gordon has done, and I am pleased to associate this group with the expression of appreciation voiced by the Prime Minister.

speechtext: The committee is considering section 3.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
Last evening when we
adjourned the discussion in committee I was asked to give consideration to possible amendments in section 4, after having had section 3 stand for the purpose of considering such amendments to section 4. Before dealing with the amendments I was asked to give a legal opinion on the meaning of the word "may" in the section. I have that legal opinion and will read it:
Legal interpretation of the word "may", law dictionary by John
May: is permitted to, has liberty to. In interpreting statutes the word may should be construed as equivalent to shall or must in cases where the good sense of the entire enactment requires it, wherever it is necessary in order to carry out the intention of the legislation, where it is necessary for the preservation or enforcement of the rights and interests of the public or third persons-
And certain authorities are given.
-but not for the purpose of creating or determining the character of rights. Where there is anything in the connection of the language or in the sense and policy of the provision to require unusual interpretation, it is used as merely permissive and discretionary.
That is the legal opinion under which the draftsmen in the department used the term "may" in these different sections.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: So that if the house wishes to make it certain that the government shall do something it should use the word "shall" instead of "may." Is not that so?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: That is not what it says.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: But that is what it means.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
I was going to say with regard to this section that I have no objection to the word being "shall" instead of "may" in this particular provision. But a proposal has been made that we amend section 4, and before going on to deal with that I wish to take 3 and 4 together because they were discussed together last evening. I suggested yesterday that we could take all the powers away from the minister and from the government except those having to do with agreements which have already been made, and all we would require to do, I think, is to amend section 3, subsection (a), by stating:
Subject to any regulations that may be made by the governor in council, the minister may
(a)	sell or export agricultural products to the government of any country or any agency thereof pursuant to any agreement already entered into.
Instead of using the word "made", use the words "already entered into", in line 3 of subsection (a). If that were done it would limit the powers given in section 3 to contracts that have already been entered into, which contracts are in the terms of the orders in council that have been discussed in the house. In carrying those out, the last three subsections deal with something somewhat different from what is covered by (a).
(b)	On behalf of the government of any country or any agency thereof purchase or negotiate contracts for the purchase of agricultural products.
That is, in carrying out the powers given under regulations by the governor in council we may purchase commodities for other governments.
(c)	By order require any person to give such information respecting his facilities for the storing or processing of agricultural products and at such times as the minister may designate in such order.
Agricultural Products Act

Then (d):
Enter into contracts for the storing or processing of agricultural products.
I have read that section through in order to come to section 4, which it has been proposed we should amend. I must say that the government prefers to have section 3 as it now stands; but as I said yesterday, if it is the intention of the committee to confine the government to carrying out the contracts we have with Britain, which is the all-important thing in the mind of the government, then we would accept that amendment. I am not however proposing the amendment to the committee; I am simply stating how it could be brought about. Assuming that section 3 will remain as it is, it has been proposed that we amend subsection one of section 4 in these words:
That subsection one of section four of the said bill be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"The governor in council shall establish one or more commodity boards with adequate producer representation and may authorize and require a commodity board to exercise and perform all or any of the powers and duties of the minister under section three of this act with reference to such agricultural products as the governor in council may designate, but in the exercise of such powers and duties a commodity board shall be subject to the direction and control of the minister.
I read that in order to call attention to w'hat would require to be done particularly in connection with subsections (c) and (d) of section 3, and I will illustrate by dealing with (d):
Enter into contracts for the storing or processing of agricultural products.
And (c):
By order require any person to give such information respecting his facilities for the storing or processing of agricultural products and at such times as the minister may designate in such order.
What we have in mind there is this. If we enter into a contract to supply bacon to Britain, that contract requires that Wiltshire sides be ordered into storage sometimes days ahead, sometimes weeks ahead, and on occasion months ahead. We order those commodities into storage in order to have them available for the loading of ships when ships can be had. There have been occasions on which it has been necessary to act the moment information is obtained with regard to what is happening in order to see that the intentions are carried out. That is the real reason why authority is given to the minister. If it were required that we should have a meeting of council and that the whole thing be determined before council as to whether we are to

proceed at all or not in connection with a matter of the kind, a considerable part of the product would be away beyond the position where any storage or anything else in connection with it could be ordered. So I say that to go through the process which is suggested here would make this section of the bill unworkable and impracticable in carrying out a programme of this kind.
I submit again that it is definitely set out, in the orders in council under which the agreements were made with regard to the products, that we deal largely with packing companies in connection with bacon and with cheese boards in connection with cheese. In those operations our action is taken after orders in council have been passed by the government in order to make the carrying out of the policy, whatever it is, administratively possible, and the minister is the administration agent.
Speaking of the proposed amendment, I have no objection to the word "may" after "minister" being changed to "shall". I have no objection at all to the words "with adequate producer representation" being added after the word "board". The section would then read:
The minister shall establish one or more commodity boards with adequate producer representation . . .
And then it goes on as it is now. If that is acceptable to the mover and seconder of the amendment, I shall be pleased to accept that amendment.

The minister may direct that any agricultural product designated by him may be purchased for the purpose of this act or the Agricultural Prices Support Act, .1944, only from a provincial marketing board.
It is suggested that the word "shall" should be used. The wording in the amendment is different, but I doubt very much whether, after I have made the explanation, the hon. member will consider the suggested wording an improvement on that of the bill itself. The suggestion is that it read: "The minister shall direct". There may be producer boards which

Agricultural Products Act
are intended to deal only with the marketing of a farm product within the bounds of a province. Most of the boards now existing are in that position. In some instances they are intended to deal only with the product of a community within the province. In many instances they do not deal with all the product which is marketed within a province. If we were compelled to order from boards of that kind all the product which we are going to export under this bill, it would not be possible for us to get the commodity which we require in the quantity in which we must have it in order to fulfil the contract. Subsection 3 says:
The minister may direct that any agricultural product designated by him may be purchased for the purpose of this act . . . only from a provincial marketing board.
Again I say that provision was included for only one purpose-and it is not required for any other purpose so far as I know-and that was for the purchase of apples or taking delivery of apples from the apple marketing board. I do not think it would improve the act, or make it possible for us to carry out as we should, the provisions of the apple agreement, to change the wording of subsection 3. Perhaps I could make my question clearer. What I want to know is what part of the total agricultural production in each year since the beginning of the war has been sold within the country and what part has been, shipped outside, and to what countries? We need that information in order to be able to discuss the sale of agricultural products. The sessional paper referred to by the minister relates only to subsidies and does not provide the information I want.

I have not the exact figures here at the moment in connection with all products for all years, but I can give proportionate figures. In the case of bacon and ham, since the war began we have sent approximately one-half the production to Great Britain. During the same period we consumed about the same amount of pork in Canada as we had consumed prior to the war. I am speaking in terms of weight. Then in the case of cheese, throughout the years we have sent to Great Britain approximately sixty per cent of our production. In two years we sent all the cheese produced in Ontario and Quebec between the months of May and October, but the average is about sixty per cent.
In so far as eggs are concerned, prior to the war we were sending, about 1.000,000 dozen. If I remember the figure correctly, that was the amount shipped the 'last year before the war and for a period of time we had been sending about that number of dozens. This year our contracts call for 83,000,000 dozen. We have sent somewhat more than that in some years but that is about the average in recent years. Those are not sent under any subsidized price; they are sent at the floor price. The floor price that is received for eggs and for cheese and bacon in Canada is the price at which these products have been secured and sent to Britain. We have been paying on cheese produced in Canada a premium of one cent a pound on cheese of 93 score and two cents a pound on cheese of 94 score. We have paid that, no matter where the cheese went. We have paid that premium directly to the producer as a quality premium, just as we have paid in the last few years a premium of $3 on A hogs and $2 on B hogs, and now it is $2 and $1 respectively. While it is true that there is no direct premium on what goes to Britain, there is a premium on all hogs produced in Canada and delivered1 to the packing houses.
Is that paid on the whole hog or on the side?

On the whole hog. It is now $2 and $1 on A and B respectively. That is paid as a premium to induce the production of a higher grade commodity. Those are the main commodities we are sending to Britain.
Before the minister leaves cheese, was there not some bonus paid on the milk that went into cheese, and was there not some provincial encouragement given as well?

Ontario gave encouragement to the production of cheese by paying one cent, and I have heard rumours that that will be raised to two cents. Quebec did pay a premium for a time and then took the premium off. It was paid on all cheese of a certain quality produced in both provinces.
It was two cents a pound on all cheese produced in Ontario.

Yes. That was paid by the provinces. We started in at a lower rate and paid a subsidy of 30 cents a hundredweight on milk entering cheese. But the British are paying that subsidy; we are not paying it. Last year the British did not pay all of it but they paid part of it. This year they are paying all the subsidy that is paid on milk entering into the production of cheese going to Britain. The Canadian consumer is not paying the subsidy on cheese produced in Canada for domestic consumption.
Was it not because there was uncertainty whether this premium was to be paid that there was such a falling off in the production of cheese in Quebec in 1946?

I am not too sure about that. We were putting forth every effort to get more butter, but you cannot get more butter and more cheese at the same time unless you increase the production of milk. The production of milk was going down slightly and, because it was going down, we could not get more of canned milk, plus cheese, plus butter. It is true that the production of butter did not stay up to the level of two years ago, nor has the production of anything else because there is not the feed to feed that there was two years ago.

The carcass meat mentioned in the table was mostly beef, which was asked about a few moments ago by the hon. member for Temis-couata. We sent 184,000,000 pounds of beef to Britain in the calendar year 1945, which is the last year for which I have the figures. That works out at 350,000 head of beef cattle in round figures, which would dress at an average of 500 pounds. The beef is in the form of frozen beef and boneless beef. We take the dressed weight and divide it into the total amount and that gives about 350,000 head of cattle. I may say that 573,000 head went out of Canada during that year, largely to Britain and European countries. The extra quantity which went to European countries went largely to UNRRA. That meat was largely in cans. It will be recalled that the year before last we took all canned meat away from the Canadian people. We did not send it to Britain but sent it to UNRRA and UNRRA distributed that beef to the different nations it was helping, largely on the European continent. The price at which these beef products have gone has again been the floor price. The meat board has been prepared at all times to take any quantity of meat that has been available in the packing houses or elsewhere across Canada at a given price, and that price is the floor price which is contained in these contracts. This meat has been sent out of Canada at that floor price. That is true of all the products of which I have been speaking. That is the reason why I have suggested in this discussion that this legislation is utilized for the purpose of putting a floor under the price of farm products. If the products can be sold at a better price for consumption in Canada they are sold for consumption in Canada, but somewhere under the ceilings which have been put on.

I do not wish to interrupt the continuity of the argument that is going on, but I have something entirely different from what we have been talking about. I should like to ask the minister this question, and if he prefers to answer it at some future time that will be all right with me. I believe this is the proper place to ask it because it involves feed and there is a principle involved. The commodity board has certain powers pursuant to the Agricultural Prices Support Act. The reason I ask the question is that I have an inquiry from a certain organization in my constituency. It is based upon an article that appeared in "The Country Guide." Why are products sold in foreign countries cheaper than they are sold here? I shall read the little statement from the article, and perhaps the minister can answer it.
The difference between export and domestic rail rates was so high, that western feed could be sold in Denmark for less than it could be sold in Saint John, New Brunswick. The Canadian freight tariff structure was in effect a system for bonusing the Danish feeder against competition by eastern Canadian hog growers.
What is the explanation for this? If the minister cares to answer it now it will be all right; if not, perhaps he can tell me when I may ask the question.

As I understood it,
the first part of the question is why the commodities that are dealt with in these contracts are sold at lower prices to the British in
Canada, delivered at a port, than they are sold in Canada to Canadians. The answer to that is the one I gave a few moments ago, that we have had not only a ceiling price in Canada but a floor price. So far as farm commodities are concerned, the floor prices since the beginning of the war have been established by the British agreements. Under these agreements we have undertaken to take delivery of all the surplus farm production in Canada at the floor price, which is the price contained in the contracts. In the case of beef that cannot be lower than half a cent a pound on red and blue beef below the Canadian price. It is one-quarter of a cent now; it was half a cent up to this year. On the lower grades of beef the margin is wider. The	floor	price	established onbacon and	ham	has	established the floorbasis in Canada not only for meat but for cattle and	hogs. It	would	be somewhatdifficult to state exactly what that floor price is at the different markets, but we have kept a record of it all across Canada during the war and, wherever we have noticed that it was tending to drop below what we considered was a reasonable floor price in relation to prices in the British contracts, we have insisted on	the	price	being	maintained on
that level. There have been only very short periods at any time during the war when the prices have not been attained either at that level or at a higher level, so that the floor prices are the prices at *which the commodities have been supplied to Britain, and in Canada they have sold between the ceiling and the floor.
If that is the floor price what is the ceiling?

I would have to get
the prices board records of the ceilings, which are different prices on different cuts of beef and pork.

I have heard the statement made many times, and probably I have made it myself sometimes that feed grain can be purchased in China at a lower rate than it can be purchased in British Columbia. I think this statement is correct, although I would want to check it up. It is made often and by

people who ought to know, that the freight rate on grain going by boat from western Canada to Denmark or to Great Britain-[DOT] it is based on the British figure rather than on the Danish figure, but if it is exported it goes on the same rate no matter to which place it goes-is much lower than the rate on grain that is to be unloaded and fed in this country. It has been said many times that the freight rate on grain from here over to Denmark and back again would not be as high, if you were able to get it that way, as it is if you ship it direct. I say again, I am repeating a statement made recently in Winnipeg by the deputy minister of New Brunswick, and it was repeated by others. Some who ought to know have said to me since that time that there is some truth in the statement, but I doubt whether it has been possible to buy grain, after it has gone over and been shipped back, at as low a price here. Whether the Danish people get it at a lower price I also doubt very much, because other things enter into the cost besides the freight rate itself.

I understand that the Department of Agriculture is a complete unit, and in this bill there is some reference to advisers whom the minister may choose. The question I wish to ask has reference to food commodities. Does the minister establish prices after consulting with his own advisers, or does he ask the wartime prices and trade board to fix prices for the Department of Agriculture? That is the first question I should like the minister to answer if he pleases.

To answer the last question first, the wartime prices and trade board ever since 1941 has set ceiling prices on food commodities that are consumed in Canada, and those of course come largely from the farms of Canada. The board has not set these prices without consultation with the Department of Agriculture. There has always been consultation with the department before the prices were set, but they had the final authority to recommend to council, and the prices were set after discussions, first as between the prices board and representatives of the Department of Agriculture, and representatives of farm organizations. The prices board has always had an advisory committee, on each of the important farm products, which has been called in and the matter has been discussed from time to time. In addition to that, we have had a committee advisory to the food board. The food board is composed entirely of agricultural departmental officials, and the prices board and Department of Trade and

Commerce officials and that board has had an advisory committee. The chairman of the advisory committee to that board is the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Each province was asked to name a representative on that committee and they named nine men. Most of the provinces named their deputy ministers, but some of them named representatives of farm organizations. Then we asked the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to nominate three; that is to say, two in addition to their president, which made a total committee of twelve. We accepted those nominations and had those men appointed.
There have been changes. The first member of the board from Quebec was Mr. McArthur, but he took on other work later and therefore resigned and someone else was appointed on the recommendation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. We have never refused to take their nominations for these positions. We have the authority to refuse, but we have never found it necessary to do so.
We are setting up a new food board and have given the Canadian Federation of Agriculture the right to select another two from western Canada and another two from eastern Canada. These recommendations have been made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, which will increase the advisory board to sixteen, seven of whom will be representatives of the Canadian federation.
The method under which that board operates is this. Whenever the chairmen of the board think they ought to have a meeting they come to the department, and to me as minister, and suggest a date. The president came yesterday, as I said last night, and suggested that we meet the first week after the Easter holidays to discuss suggestions which the government hopes to place before the country with regard to prices or any other matters that may concern the production of farm commodities.
We are not bound by the advice we receive, and the advice given is not a one-way street. Meetings are held behind closed doors. The representatives of the province and the farm organizations talk quite freely to us and we talk quite freely to them. Up to date we have been able to reach an agreement on the things that have been done by the government, with the result that no criticism has been made by those who have been members of that organization. Some others have desired to get on that organization and we have made provision whereby some of them can get on, provided that they are acceptable to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. We have now the recommendation for the four additional to go on.

That board will meet, and it may be one of the reasons why it will be most difficult for us to make announcements early with regard to the prices of dairy products. We wish to have the advice of that organization. We want them to know what the reasons are for any action we find it necessary to take, in order that they may advise their own organization accordingly, and after we have had these discussions we hope to make the announcements as soon as possible.
I made a similar suggestion with regard to the announcements about feed grain. The main reason why we wanted to hold it up until we had met the farm organization was to have their advice before making a decision. We did not decide to do what they asked us to do, as is obvious. They asked us to pay an average bonus on feed grains. We increased the price, and the reason I give the house and the country for that is this. The condition which was outlined when the first recommendation v'as made was found to be impracticable of continuation, and therefore we took the alternative suggestion of the farm organizations when we brought down the official decision as to what ought to be done. So that we have been proceeding by obtaining advice and using it where, after having heard all their arguments, we think it wise to follow that advice, and trying to convince them, where we thought it wras not wise to follow their suggestions. that some other course ought to be adopted. Up to date we have arrived at understandings.

Just one or two questions. From what the right hon. gentleman has said, I understand that prices of agricultural products for home consumption are established by the prices board. The first question I wish to ask is whether prices for agricultural exports are established under the authority of the Department of Agriculture.
Floor prices have been established under the authority of the Department of Agriculture.
Yes.
Ceiling prices have been established under the authority of the prices board.

Thank you. My last question is this. Will the minister be kind enough to put on record on Hansard a list of the commitments actually in force regarding the shipments of agricultural products to other countries, by class or category of commodity?
Mr. Chairman-
Just a minute. I want an answer; after I have obtained it, the hon. member may have the floor for the whole afternoon.
They are here somewhere. I wonder if the hon. member would permit another question to be asked in the meantime.
Yes.

I asked the minister a few moments ago the price which the grower in Prince Edward Island was receiving for potatoes under the British order. He quoted me a price of $1.15. Does that include the bag and the tag?
No. I stated at the time that it was just for the potatoes.

I wonder if we could possibly get a little closer to the bill which is before us this afternoon. I should like to ask the minister if he recalls that yesterday, while he was answering some questions I asked, he had this to say, as reported at page 1491 of Hansard, with respect to an act passed by this parliament in 1939 to assist in the formation and encouragement of cooperatives. He was pointing out that some of these organizations could be made use of under this act, and he said:
I was looking in my file for the return that was brought down a few days ago indicating the number of organizations which have been set up under that legislation since 1939.
Would the minister be good enough to give us the number of that return so that we might look it up; or, if he has not it with him, will he have his secretary advise us what it is?
When the minister was replying to the hon. member for Kootenay West, in referring to the provincial boards which were under discussion at that time, he said, as reported at page 1504 of Hansard:
It is with a small "p," a provincial marketing board. There may be a dozen in one province dealing with different products.
As the minister says, there may be a dozen of these organizations in a province dealing with different commodities. That part I can understand. But can there be a board or organization set up under provincial legislation setting up marketing boards, and at the same time can those boards or organizations obtain assistance from the federal government? And can those boards, by the board set up under this act, be delegated or designated as the agency for the federal government?
Agricultural Products Act

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a question of order. I respect the views of my hon. colleagues, but there is nothing more in order than a question with regard to what is to be done by virtue of a bill, and my hon. friend knows that. We do not want to be left in the dark. The minister seems to be willing to give the information, and I will ask him again if he will be kind enough to answer my last question, which was in regard to the actual commitments regarding shipments of food to any other country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I might inform the hon. member for Temiscouata that I did not rule his question out of order. I did not know the question had been raised.

No; it is not that at all. This is a vital question, and one which is perfectly relevant. The hon. member who just spoke said that, he would come to the nucleus or the marrow of the bill by asking another question. I want to know what is to be done with this bill. Of course my faith is not the same as that of the hon. member for Humboldt. He believes in things which I do not believe in. I am not going to repeat today what I said yesterday. Today we are to have answers giving facts, and the minister is willing to answer. The minister did not refuse to answer, but the hon. member for Humboldt tried to change the course of the discussion by intervening at the wrong moment. I think we should proceed in committee in just the same manner as we proceed in court. When one has the floor, he has an opportunity of following the line of his questioning. I did not rise on a point of order at all regarding your ruling, Mr. Chairman, because you did not make one, and no one asked you to make one. But I rise to a point of order and a question of privilege at the same time; because when a member rises in the house to ask a question of a minister, and the minister is willing to reply and looks in his file for the information with which to answer, I do not see why he should not be allowed to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a question of privilege. If it was the innocent remark that I made which has sent the hon. member for Temiscouata off on another tirade, I am quite prepared to withdraw it. I say it is a sad day indeed if an hon. member cannot rise and suggest that we get a little closer to the bill under consideration.

I will tell the hon. gentleman that I was not offended at all, but I regret very much not having the information. I want the information; and if he rose to

prevent me from getting it, let me tell him that I will stand up until I do get it, because the minister is willing to give it. I do not see why any member distracts the attention of the minister when he is ready to answer a question, and I am sure the minister will answer my question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I understand the minister requested that we proceed with further questions while he was looking up certain information. If the minister has the information now, I am sure he will answer the question.
Thank you.

The information is here, Mr. Chairman. My officials are looking through a pile of information here trying to find what is required, but they have not yet located it. I will give it to my hon. friend as soon as I locate it.
I thank the minister very much.
He said that ten minutes ago.
The minister was willing to answer, and I wanted to have the answer, whether now or a little later on.

I am bound to agree that the hon. member for Temiscouata has been very much in order in asking his questions this afternoon, and I think the remarks which were made by the hon. member for Humboldt, and which precipitated this little argument, were quite uncalled for. I understood there was agreement between the hon. member for Temiscouata and the minister that the officials were looking for the information in order that the answer might be given, and that the minister invited further questions in the meantime.
I have two related questions which I should like to ask the minister as a result of questions from producers in my part of the country. The first is this: Have Canada Packers a representative on the meat board and on the wartime prices and trade board? If so, who is the official. If the minister has that information, then I am sure he can give me some enlightenment on the next question which I wish to ask; and I shall give a concrete example.
On the Winnipeg live stock market, according to the minister's own report for February 8, finished steers were selling for fifteen cents a pound, live weight. Some weeks later than that-I have not the exact date before me-the

Agricultural Products Act
wartime prices and trade board officials announced an increase of approximately three cents a pound for dressed beef. Since that time, live beef on the Winnipeg live stock market is selling for, on an average, one cent a pound less for the same quality beef. Could the minister give me a reasonable explanation which I can pass on to the producers, who are wondering why this has taken place, under the present regulations.
Would the hon. member repeat the latter part of the example he has given.

I pointed out that on February 8 the price prevailing, according to the minister's report, was fifteen cents a pound on finished steers. Some weeks later an announcement was made by the wartime prices and trade board officials to the effect that dressed beef would increase in price to the extent of three cents a pound, varying, of course, according to the different cuts. Since that time, and right up to date, the same type of live beef has been selling for approximately one cent a pound less than it was prior to that announcement. The producers are wondering why that has taken place, in view of the regulations and controls of today. I am sure if the packers have a representative on the meat board or on the wartime prices and trade board that representative will be able to give an explanation that I could pass on to these people.

The meat board is composed of Mr. Taggart, who is chairman. Then there is Mr. L. W. Pearsall, who is manager, and Mr. S. E. Todd, who is managing director of the industrial and development council of the Canadian meat packers, and who is a board member. I presume he is the gentleman to whom reference has been made. He was secretary of the food board during the first war, and during the war just past he was on the meat board.
Then there is Mr. McOuat, who is general agricultural agent for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and is also on the board. The secretary is Mr. P. E. Light, chief of the live stock and poultry marketing division. It will be noted that Mr. Taggart is chairman and Mr. Pearsall is manager.
Those are not the names I had in mind. I think Canada Packers still has another representative on the wartime prices and trade board, if he is not on the meat board.

Canada Packers, as such, have no representative on the meat board. But
the packing organization as a whole, which is the organization from which we must get our bacon and hams, have a member on the board.
They might have a representative on the wartime prices and trade board, apart from the meat board, might they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have never heard of any representative of Canada Packers on the wartime prices and trade board. Certainly there is none in the membership of the board. They may have selected some administrator who, before his selection, worked for Canada Packers, or something of that kind. But it would not be a very high up official.
Could the minister give me an answer?

I would have to search the record, or have it searched, I am not in a position to answer the question as to the level of prices; and I take it that is what is wanted, from what has been said. But there are a great many things that can be said about the level of prices on a certain day depending upon the type of cattle on the market. I would not like to say that, because prices were at different levels, everything is explained. But the fact is that the board all through the war, and even now, has kept a close check on the activities in different markets in connection with live stock products. Up to date it has succeeded in maintaining returns to the farmer at the floor.
We have never attempted to keep them down. There are times when they go above what we would consider to be the ceiling. I suppose that is done because probably the packing plant is prepared to take a loss, or at the most a small profit over a period of time in order to supply its customers. They even pay higher prices for live cattle than the ceiling would permit. They claim to have sold at a loss at different times. Then, when there are greater supplies on the market they may sell closer to the floor. During that period of time they would make up the losses which they previously incurred. I assume that is the condition under which they operate. I should think it would be the natural condition under which to operate. But to our knowledge, prices have not gone below the floor in connection with this matter.

Is it fair to assume that the amount of dressed beef in storage might enter into the picture, for some period of time? I was thinking that your board would have a reasonable explanation for that. For instance, if there were a great amount of dressed beef in storage, that might be the
Agricultural Products Act

answer, over a period of time. I should think there would be some reasonable explanation for the situation.
This raises a very sore point with the farmers.
Just a minute; wait until I have a reply.

I am told that the answer that can be given by the board is this: Perhaps hon. members have noticed that in the press, for two or three weeks before the announcement was finally made, there were rumours to the effect that this would be done. I presume that what the hon. member is suggesting is that, if there were a member who was a representative from the packers on the board, they might have got knowledge of that. But from what I know of what goes on around Ottawa, I am sure that they did not require to have a member on the board in order to find out.
I am not making any suggestion.

Most of the things
decided in our boards and most of the things decided by the government are in the papers before decisions are finally reached. They may be only rumours. But there are a lot of people who have seen it happen so often that they are quite prepared to accept the rumours and take a chance on them. I understand that the price of beef did go up some days before this change was made, and this made it impossible to go up as much as it would have gone, if it had been affected only by this one price rise.

I was not making any suggestion. I was looking for an answer. If these officials who had experience were on the board, or on the wartime prices and trade board, they would have a logical answer to it, something which the ordinary layman does not know anything about.
You will not get anything answered over there.

I do not want to get away off the bill, but I should like to clear this matter up. I am keenly interested in the point the hon. member for Souris has just raised. The trouble is that the packer has a ceiling, but the farmer has no ceiling. There is no ceiling on live steers today, And the packer can pay for them whatever he darned well likes.
Oh, oh.
Oh, you fellows have said lots worse than that.
That is nothing to what your constituents say about the government, eh?

The minister knows that the wartime prices and trade board has a ceiling on dressed beef. Then that is when the meat board steps in, whenever it does not make that price. You or I can take a carload of steers to the market tomorrow. If we do not like what the packer gives us for them we can take them home again. There is no protection for us from the meat board.
We have a situation today where the farmer has no protection from the ceiling. We know that if we take a 12 or 13-cent steer it will turn into 20 or 20|-cent beef, according to dressing. When we appeal to the meat board and say that we are not receiving the protection to which we are entitled, they tell us, "Well, put your beef on the rail, and we will see what they will make." They are going to force us to rail-grade them. I for one will never agree to rail-grading of beef, although I agree with the minister that that is the proper way to grade it. But it is not the proper way as long as it is so definitely in the hands of the meat packers.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall section 4 as
amended carry?

I rise to a question of privilege which it will take me but a minute to discuss. I notice in the Ottawa Journal of this evening that John Strachey is denying in Manchester, England, what I said yesterday in the house. I have here a clipping from the Montreal Gazette of Friday, March 15, 1935, which quotes a Chicago dispatch of the Associated Press, in which Mr. Strachey is reported as saying:
I am not a communist, but a believer in communist theories.

I wonder if what the hon. member is saying has anything to do with this .bill. I cannot see anything in section 4 dealing with Mr. Strachey, the minister of food in Great Britain, nor can I see anything in that section of the bill that has any reference to what his opinions are with regard to communism or any other ism.

The rules of the house say that a question of privilege may be raised at any time. I am sorry to interrupt the discussion, but I shall not be long. I simply want to answer this person who denied what I said in the house. If my hon. friend looks at the small book he will find that that is one of the first rules. I quote what Mr. Strachey said:

Agricultural Products Act
I am not a communist, but a believer in communist theories. I am primarily an author. Being a communist is a full time job and I can't spare the time for it. Besides, anyone who would advocate overthrowing the United States government is crazy. I make no secret of my economic opinions. I entirely deny the charges that have been preferred against me. I am not an anarchist so you can all sleep safe and sound in your beds tonight.
I am sure that no one will consider him dangerous. I do not consider him seriously at all, and that is why I object to any transactions being made by the Canadian government with him. I protest strongly against it.

I should like to refer again to subsections 2 and 3 of section 4 about which I spoke yesterday. Apparently the commodity boards which are to be established will be established under section 9 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944, but I think we are faced with the possibility that that act might be declared unconstitutional. I find that that act is headed:
An act for the support of the prices of agricultural products during the transition from war to peace.
Apparently it is only a temporary act. I wish to know if that act has been incorporated in any permanent act. If it has, I should like to know how it could be, since it refers only to keeping up prices in a province. It does not refer to interprovincial or foreign trade and it could not be made permanent. I am afraid that you will find that any board appointed will have no power. There is nothing in this act that would give it any status. I am afraid that, by the terms of this section, you will be appointing something that cannot in fact exist.

Subsection 1 of section 4 gives authority to appoint commodity boards or to utilize any commodity board that does exist. There are no commodity boards that have been set up under the other act. What we are anticipating might happen as we go along is that some of these products may be taken out from under these boards and placed partly under other boards. If we had commodity boards under the other act handling those products, then we could appoint those boards to deal with this act as well. We have not any of them and we do not know that we shall have any. This act is temporary, being only for one year, while the other act is for a much longer period. It is not as temporary as this one.
This is for only a year, but the other act must fall right away because-
The other act is more permanent than this.
You think it is.
The other act was placed on the statute books in 1944 and it remains there until this house takes it off.

It remains there until some court of law declares it is unconstitutional because it is no longer necessary because of any emergency. The only reason for its being there was the emergency created in the change from war to peace.
It was passed by this house; it was not under the War Measures Act.
Has it ever been brought in?
Yes.
On what date?
April 1 last. It is being utilized in connection with the provision of funds.

I rise to a question of privilege and I am sorry the hon. member for Temiscouata has left the chamber. The question of privilege raised by the hon. member was not a question of privilege. Under the guise of its being a question of privilege he was taking the opportunity to protest against making a deal with a minister of the British crown. I ask that that be stricken from the record because it is not a question of privilege at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question should have been raised earlier.
I have been trying to catch your eye, but I could not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member could have risen at any time on a question of privilege.

He thinks that two
wrongs make a right.

The minister has said that the Agricultural Prices Support Act was proclaimed last April. Is it not a fact that all the purchases of apples which we heard about this afternoon were made under that act? If I recall correctly I have seen reference to this in the public accounts.
No apples were purchased under that act. The apples were purchased under the War Measures Act to complete an agreement made under the War Measures Act by order in council.

What would happen in this hypothetical case? You are using a board set
Agricultural Products Act

up under this act to support prices, but this act does not come up next year; it is simply allowed to drop.
I am hoping I shall not have to wait as long to get it through at the next session as we have had to wait this session. I think we should leave the argument about that until the next session.
Why not make it a little more permanent?
Was subsection 3 of section 4 amended in any way?

No, it has not been amended in any way up to the moment. I think the hon. member asked us to let it stand until we had finished with section 4. We are trying to complete section 4 and then we shall go back to section 3.

I had an amendment to that particular subsection which I intended to bring forward, but in view of the amendment brought forward by the hon. member for Peace River I do not know whether this would be of any use. However I should like to hear what the minister has to say about it. It is:
That subsection 3 of section 4 be repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"Notwithstanding anything in this or any other act contained producer boards set up under provincial marketing acts, where such boards exist or may from time to time be brought into existence, shall be used for the purpose of this act, or the Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944."
I would think that amendment has the same meaning as the one that was withdrawn.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member is moving this amendment?
Yes, I am moving it.

I do not know whether the hon. member was in the house when I was dealing with the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Peace River, but this one would have exactly the same effect, though its wording is not exactly the same. What I stated at that time was that there are very few, if any, boards set up in Canada which handle all of a particular product. It might be said that the apple board handles all the apples that are exported, but there is no authority in this bill yet, and will not be unless we accept the amendment I am proposing to section
5.	that would put the apple board in a position to do what is proposed. There is an egg board in Alberta, and that is the nearest approach to such a board. What I stated on the other amendment I state again now, that where 
these boards do control the marketing of farm products, there is nowhere else we can go to get that product. On the other hand, some of these boards are set up to market products within a province, and others deal only wdth marketing part of the product within a province. But these British agreements we have to carry on from day to day and week to wedk, and we cannot wait for these boards to be enlarged to get the product we want from a particular province. We must go to organizations already set up to handle them. If we accepted an amendment that, wherever there is a board, we must buy from that board it would defeat the very purpose of the bill, which is to get all the surplus food that is available in a given area, in a given province or in the whole dominion, to enable us to fill these contracts. If there is such a board in existence anywhere we shall do exactly with that board what we propose to do with the apple board. We shall take our products from that board. But I would not want to be compelled to deal only with that board, if there is such a board in existence. It may not be able to deliver the surplus of a province at all.
The minister says he would deal with the board but he does not want to be bound to do it.

I am saying that the amendment would bind me. If there is a board in Ontario that handles and markets half of the apples in Ontario-I shall not get into any difficulties by mentioning apples because it is not a product being exported-I would be compelled to go to that board to get the surplus of apples in Ontario if we wanted to market Ontario apples. But those people may not want to market any apples outside Ontario, and there may be a good reason for that. Ontario is the best market for apples in Canada, and they may not want to market their apples outside the province. I do not want to be compelled to go to that board and take their apples away from them. We want to utilize these boards where they exist to do the job that has to be done, but we do not want to go beyond that.
The only alternative would be for the minister to requisition the apples, to get the apples before they came under the control of the board.

I hope we are not going to have to requisition anything. The only reason there is authority here to requisition is that we might want a product like Wiltshire sides, and the packing plant may say: "We can sell these to better advantage Somewhere

Agricultural Products Act
else and we are not going to sell them to you." Under those circumstances we ought to have authority to say that a certain percentage of the product must be put into the brine now and cured in order to go into bacon. That has to be done weeks ahead. That is what the power will be utilized for. But as for taking commodities away from small dealers or from small cooperatives or small producer organizations, we do not want to exercise that kind of authority at all and we do not intend to exercise it.

I agree entirely with the minister's suggestion. But surely it follows, if the board wants to help you carry out these contracts, they are not going to try to beat the minister and sell somewhere else, provided that the price is reasonable. I understand that the minister has agreed to consult the producers in setting the price. Therefore we have a reasonable assurance that the price will be reasonable and just. If that is the case, the boards are not going to try to beat the minister to it by making it impossible for him to get the products to fill the contracts. A big packing plant might, but I doubt that too. That being the case, why will the minister not accept the suggestion that he deal through a board where a board exists, and then, where a board does not exist, he can go into the market himself and set up whatever agency is necessary.
Where a board does exist it may not have the product we want.
Then you do not use that board.

But the amendment
would compel me to take the product from that board and from no one else. In other words, if somebody were to set up a board in Ontario to market the producers' bacon, then under the amendment we would have to take the product from that board. But the proper place to take the bacon from, under present conditions and under any conditions that I can foresee while these agreements are running, is the packing plant. There is no one else in a position to market it. To say that I must deal with a board because somebody has set up a small board and said, "We are going to market this product"-it just is not possible to do that kind of thing.

There would be no objection to putting in a reasonable definition of "producer board" if the minister is afraid of that situation arising But for him to say that, because somebody may set up a board and call it a producer board, therefore he will have to deal with that board, is not 83166-98
a sound argument against the principle we are advocating. We have had a good deal of argument about this, but we thought we would make one more effort to have the minister accept the principle we are advocating. I have his answer now, and so far as I am concerned I have nothing more to say.

I ask leave, Mr. Chairman, to withdraw my amendment.
Amendment withdrawn.

May I ask the
minister if section 4 has been amended in any particular at all? There have been amendments advanced and withdrawn until it is difficult to know the extent to which amendments have been accepted or rejected.

The amendment which was accepted was to subsection 1 of section 4 and was to this effect, that the minister shall establish one or more commodity boards with adequate producer representation. That is the only amendment that has been accepted.

I have listened
to the arguments advanced. I do not. know whether any arguments advanced can have any effect, but I do not recall any instance either in the Natural Products Marketing Act-and I have it here and am ready to discuss it-or in any other act where a minister has asked parliament to anoint him with the powers which the minister asks for in this bill.

May I repeat what I
said when the hon. member was not here. If the hon. member wants to follow that argument further I suggest that he amend section 3 by inserting the words "already entered into", and then I shall not have the powers he complains of. The only reason I need these powers is to do what I am asked to do by the other side of the house.
When the minister starts advancing an amendment witn such anxiety I begin to wonder what is behind the suggestion and the anxiety he has. I am not going to deal with that at all.
I do not want any extra power. That is the only anxiety.

I am glad to see that the minister does not want any extra power. Therefore I am going to suggest that the minister should not be the one to establish one or more commodity boards to carry out the powers and direction and controls to be exercised by him. The authority to appoint those boards invariably rests in the governor in council.

It is there.

Agricultural Products Act

Oh, no; that is the point. Section 4 (1) says:
The minister may establish one or more commodity boards . . .
While the minister says that only the governor in council can establish these boards, that is not what the bill says. The only power of the governor in council is in section 5 (1), which says:
The governor in council may make regulations for carrying any of the purposes or provisions of this act into effect . . .
It does not refer to the making of appointments. The only appointments that the governor in council has anything to do with are provided by section 7 (1) which says:
The minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, employ such professional, technical or other officers, clerks and employees as are necessary for the proper administration of this act and fix their remuneration.
That is all. The establishment of the boards is not in the hands of the governor in council. Apparently the minister thought it was because, when he interrupted me a moment ago, he said that the bill so provides. The appointment of the boards is in the exclusive hands of the minister. In view of the fact that he thought the bill provided that it was in the hands of the governor in council, I suggest that section 4 (1) be amended in this particular, that where the word "minister" appears in line twenty-four the words "governor in council" be substituted. That is a reasonable suggestion and I think the minister will accept it.
To shorten up the argument, may I point out that the only authority which I have in this bill in connection with these matters is given to me by section 3.
No.

In that section the gov ernor in council does make the regulations under which I operate. It simply states that I may pass it on to the commodity boards. The boards are then set up. I have no objection to putting in the words "governor in council". Let us put them in and get it over with.

Not to get it over with, but because it is necessary.
' Mr. WRIGHT: That is exactly the way our amendment read when the minister asked that it be changed.

We shall accept it. Let us get on with the bill. Apparently some hon.

members are more interested in six o'clock than they are in getting on with the bill. Let us get through with this section and get on.
I move that the words "governor in council" be substituted for the word "minister" which appears on line twenty-four of subsection 1 of section 4.

Amendment agreed to.
Subsection as amended agreed to.
Section 4 as amended agreed to

We now come to section 3, and I wish to refer to the preamble in order to discuss the section. The minister has said that he is anxious to get this bill through. I have listened almost continuously, except for an hour or so last evening, to what has taken place and have taken no part in the argument. Therefore I ask the indulgence of the committee at this time. The preamble sets forth the reason for the bill. It states that the reason for it is that certain agreements will continue in force and that for the purpose of enabling Canada to carry out these agreements the bill is being introduced.
The minister will admit that under section 3 the powers are unusually wide; that they could not be wider than those contained in the section if the minister had spent all his time in endeavouring to draft omnipotent powers. He has already told the committee that he was prepared to restrict them to any agreement already entered into. But aside altogether from that, the powers asked for are no less than and no greater than those under the communist government of Yugoslavia.
Or the Bennett government of 1934.

I have heard much about the Bennett government. I have the act here and I would be ready to discuss it. As a matter of fact, that act was declared beyond the powers of parliament because of what it asked for. If the committee wish to discuss that act mayr I say that the powers asked for in it are infinitely less than anything asked for in this bill.

May I submit this for my hon. friend's attention. In regard to the other power which is conferred on the minister, namely, the power to make further agreements at his will, I suggest that is placing in him altogether too great a power. In other words, he continues to make agreements without consultation with parliament and without regard to prices which are determined upon. We have had this experience before, for instance, in connection with the wheat agreement. We are now about to enter into the field of an international wheat agreement. The government enters into an agreement, binds the country, and then comes back to parliament and says, ''we require enabling legislation in order to support the contracts which we have entered into". All that amounts to, sir, is making parliament a pawn in the minister's hands to carry out the agreements that he makes, independent of parliament, without consultation with parliament and without permitting parliament to consider the prices, whether fair or unfair.
I just want to ask my hon. friend this simple question; at least to me it is a simple one. How would he expect 243 people to negotiate an agreement of this kind?

Let us in this case endeavour to restore to parliament its rightful place instead of turning over to a minister arbitrary and uncontrolled powers; for under this bill and under this section parliament is asked to show the greatest manifestation of faith in one man that any parliament has ever been asked to.
I come now to the question of the legality or illegality of this legislation. I shall refer to a case in point, because I should like to hear-and I am sure the committee would- my right hon. friend, the Minister of Justice, expounding the proposition upon which parliament is being asked to pass this legislation which is similar in part to that declared ultra vires in 1937, particularly having regard to the
decision in the case of Attorney General of Ontario and Canada Temperance Federation, which is reported in 1946 Appeal Cases at page 193. I read in part from that judgment, dealing as it does with the question of emergency which heretofore lawyers have believed justified parliament in passing legislation which, in its essence, infringes on the rights of the province under provincial jurisdiction of property and civil rights. This is what the head-note says:
The British North America Act, 1867, nowhere gives power to the dominion parliament to legislate in matters which are properly within the competence of the provincial legislatures merely because of the existence of an emergency.
And I repeat those words, "merely because of the existence of an emergency."
An emergency may be the occasion which calls for legislation, but it is the nature of the legislation itself, and not the existence of emergency, that must determine whether it is valid or not. The true test must be found in the real subject matter of the legislation; if it is such that it goes beyond local or provincial concern or interests and must, from its inherent nature, be a concern of the dominion as a whole, then it will fall within the competence of the dominion parliament as a matter affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada, though it may in another aspect touch on matters specially reserved to the provincial legislatures.
The next portion of the head-note deals with the particular case. Having regard to the extraordinary powers which are asked for and what has happened to similar legislation in the past, I think the Minister of Justice might well, at the earliest possible moment, place before the committee and the country the attitude of the Department of Justice in regard to this bill and other similar emergency and extraordinary legislation.
